Subject: Performance SLOs — Context window / max tokens and latency impact (post-call recap)

Hi Alyssa — thanks again for the call earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have alignment: 

Summary of requirements from the call:
- 99th percentile tail latency target: <= 200ms for typical read-only assistant flows (avg input ~600 tokens, output <= 256 tokens).
- Peak throughput target: 150 reqs/sec with concurrency of ~40 sustained, bursts to 250 for short windows.
- Streaming: customer-visible partial tokens are required for the chat UI (progressive rendering).
- Context window: many of your cases require 8k–16k input windows (longer threads + attachments parsed). Some occasional 32k sessions for batch analytics.
- Max token output: typically 256, but some endpoints may request up to 1024 for summarization jobs.

Open questions we should validate/confirm:
1) What fraction of calls will hit >8k context vs <=8k? You mentioned ~20% long-form.
2) Are the 32k sessions expected to be synchronous (interactive) or async batch?
3) Tolerance for client-perceived latency vs server-side total tokens generated (ie streaming can mask longer generation times).

Next steps I propose:
- Alyssa to share a sample prompt set + traffic shape (p95/p99 rates over a day).
- We’ll run a benchmark plan (model selection, batching, and streaming experiment) and return a latency/throughput estimate for the three context sizes: 8k, 16k, 32k.
- Internal engineering sync to map config to Dedicated vs Hosted options and expected cost delta.

I’ve CC’d Rachel (Prod Eng) and Marcus (Solutions) to validate latency modeling and propose concrete config suggestions.

Thanks — I’ll follow up with a calendar invite for an engineering sync after we get your samples.

— Marissa

Hi all — quick pass from Prod Eng with a conservative latency model. Attached CSV contains the estimates (latency_estimates.csv). High-level summary below.

Assumptions / baseline config:
- Model: redwood-medium-32k (float16) for interactive; redwood-large-32k for high-quality async summarization.
- Quantization: prefer fp16 for interactive to maintain latency; int8/4 for batch summarization to lower cost when quality tolerates it.
- Batching: steady-state batching window 5–10ms for interactive flows; larger micro-batches for async.
- Streaming: progressive token streaming reduces perceived latency for the user but server-side total generation time largely unchanged — helps interactive UX for large outputs.

Latency estimates (selected rows):
- 8k context, 256 output tokens: p50 ~40ms, p95 ~120ms, p99 ~190ms (with continuous batching + streaming).
- 16k context, 256 output tokens: p50 ~85ms, p95 ~220ms, p99 ~420ms (streaming improves UX; backend still spends more time).
- 32k context, 256 output tokens: p50 ~220ms, p95 ~600ms, p99 ~1.2s (recommended to run 32k interactive only for targeted users; prefer async).
- 8k context, 1024 output tokens: p50 ~120ms, p95 ~420ms, p99 ~800ms (streaming strongly recommended).

Throughput / sizing notes:
- We estimate ~30–40 interactive requests per A100-80GB-equivalent GPU with batching tuned to your traffic pattern; with 150 reqs/sec sustained you’d target ~4–5 GPUs for interactive headroom (plus autoscale).
- For bursts (250 rps), burst capacity or additional ephemeral nodes recommended to protect p99.

Recommendations / mitigations:
1) Cache static prefixes and KV caches for long conversations to reduce repeated attention cost.
2) Use streaming for all interactive end-points to improve perceived latency for longer outputs.
3) Route 32k jobs to async workers with quantized models to meet 60s batch SLO and lower cost.
4) Start with Dedicated reserved pool for baseline capacity + hosted burst for unexpected growth.

Next steps I propose:
- Run an A/B microbenchmark using your sample prompts to validate these numbers (need 2–4 hours to schedule and run).
- I’ll attach latency_estimates.csv to this thread. If FinCo is okay, we can schedule the microbenchmark for next week.

— Rachel
